title: Brushing up on phrasal verbs
subtitle: come across, press on, brush up on, lay off
summary: Handle phrasal verbs with confidence: learn them in context, notice how the particle shapes the meaning, and get the position of the object right.

lesson.heading: How to learn phrasal verbs
lesson.text: There are a great many phrasal verbs in English and many learners find them particularly difficult to master. The best way to learn them is in context: when you **come across** one - that is, meet it - write it down in an example sentence rather than as a bare pair of words.

examples.text: I **came across** some lovely old photos when I was sorting some boxes yesterday.
It is sensible to concentrate first on understanding phrasal verbs rather than using them.

lesson.heading: Two things to remember
lesson.text: First, one verb + particle combination may have more than one meaning: **come across** also means give an impression of being, and **come over** can be used in the same way. Second, there is usually a single-word alternative, so instead of **put forward** a plan you can *propose* a plan, and instead of **rush into** a decision you can *make a hasty decision*.

examples.text: He can **come across** as unfriendly when you first meet him.
Meena can **come across** as a little arrogant at times, but she's just shy.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with come
rows: I hope our plans to visit Russia **come off**.
travel to one place from another
Sandro's family **came over** from Italy for the wedding.
influence someone to behave in a particular way
I don't know what **came over me**.
The proposal has **come under** a lot of criticism.
If the opportunity to work in the US **comes up**, you must take it.
have to deal with a problem or difficulty
Our plan has **come up against** some obstacles.
lesson.note: A very large number of phrasal verbs are built on common verbs such as come, do, get and go.

lesson.heading: What the particle tells you: on
lesson.text: The second part of a phrasal verb is a preposition or particle, and it can help you work out the meaning. **On** often conveys the idea of continuing over a period of time.

examples.text: Selina decided to **stay on** at university and do a Master's degree.
Try not to **dwell on** the past.
examples.note: dwell on = keep thinking about, usually something unpleasant

examples.text: I didn't expect platform shoes to **catch on**.
I wish she'd stop **going on** about her new car.
examples.note: go on about = talk at length

examples.text: The weather was terrible but the climbers **pressed on** regardless.
examples.note: press on = continue in a determined way

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs at work
rows: improve knowledge of something already learnt but partly forgotten
start doing it with great energy
begin to feel relaxed and happy in a new place
prepare it by collecting information from several sources

lesson.heading: Where does the object go?
rows: brush up a skill / brush a skill up
rush into a decision, not ~~rush a decision into~~
put together a report / put a report together
lay off staff / lay staff off
call off a meeting / call a meeting off
put forward a plan / put a plan forward
lesson.note: When you learn a phrasal verb, note down where the particle and the object can go.

lesson.text: Record every new phrasal verb inside a whole sentence - the sentence stores the meaning, the grammar and the word order all at once.

exercises.prompt: Charlie was quick to take advantage of a chance for promotion that ___ at his workplace.
exercises.explanation: If an opportunity comes up, it occurs unexpectedly.

exercises.prompt: The project was going well until we ___ some legal problems.
exercises.explanation: To come up against something is to have to deal with a problem or difficulty.

exercises.prompt: I'm afraid it looks as if our plans to move to a new flat may not ___.
exercises.explanation: If a plan comes off, it happens successfully.

exercises.prompt: Something strange ___ me and I shouted at him angrily.
exercises.explanation: If something comes over you, it influences you to behave in a particular way.

exercises.prompt: Dan is always ___ on about how rich he is.
exercises.explanation: To go on about something is to talk about it at tiresome length.

exercises.prompt: You can't change what happened, so don't ___ on it.
exercises.explanation: To dwell on something is to keep thinking about it, usually something unpleasant.

exercises.prompt: We'd better ___ on if we're going to get to the hostel before dark.
exercises.explanation: To press on is to continue in a determined way.

exercises.prompt: I'm going to ___ on after work to finish the report.
exercises.explanation: To stay on is to remain somewhere longer than expected.

exercises.prompt: Taekwondo has really ___ on - all my friends are learning it.
exercises.explanation: If something catches on, it becomes popular.

exercises.prompt: Hugo's family tried their best to ___ him on to complete his novel.
exercises.explanation: To urge someone on is to encourage them.

exercises.statement: Do you think the company will have to lay any staff out?
exercises.explanation: The verb is lay off: Do you think the company will have to lay any staff off?

exercises.statement: I learnt Spanish at school but need to brush it on before I go to Spain.
exercises.explanation: The verb is brush up: I learnt Spanish at school but need to brush it up before I go to Spain.

exercises.statement: I'm putting a presentation together for the board to consider.
exercises.explanation: Correct - you can say put together a presentation or put a presentation together.

exercises.statement: Nita put forward some very interesting ideas at the meeting.
exercises.explanation: Correct - to put forward an idea is to propose it.

options: If you rush into a decision, you may regret it later.
If you rush for a decision, you may regret it later.
If you rush a decision into, you may regret it later.
If you rush on a decision, you may regret it later.
exercises.explanation: Rush into is fixed - the object cannot come between the verb and the particle.

options: I love the way Katie always throws herself into everything she does.
I love the way Katie always throws herself onto everything she does.
I love the way Katie always throws herself on everything she does.
I love the way Katie always throws herself over everything she does.
exercises.explanation: To throw yourself into something is to start doing it with great energy.

exercises.prompt: The family soon ___ their new flat in the city.
exercises.explanation: To settle in is to begin to feel relaxed and happy in a new place.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with its single-word meaning.
Can the particle go either before or after the object, or is its position fixed?

exercises.answer: I need to brush up on my computer skills
exercises.explanation: To brush up on something is to improve knowledge you once had but have partly forgotten.
